group.title: Work and careers
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The last time or day by which something must be done.
examples: The {deadline} for the report is Friday.
wrong: We finished the work a week after the deadline, so we were early.
Please do it in the deadline.

words.meaning: Money an employee gets regularly for their work.
examples: He got a higher {salary} after the promotion.
wrong: I pay my salary to the company every month.
She salaries ten thousand pesos.

words.meaning: A piece of work that is planned with a goal.
examples: Our team finished the {project} on time.
wrong: The project is a small yellow bird.
She projects a new idea last week.

words.meaning: A piece of work that must be done.
examples: Writing emails is my first {task} each day.
wrong: My task is something I never need to do.
She tasks many jobs today.

words.meaning: A plan for how much money you will spend.
examples: We need to stay within the {budget}.
wrong: We spent twice our budget, so we saved money.
He budgets a sunny river.

words.meaning: A person who is paid to work for a company.
examples: Each {employee} gets a security badge.
wrong: The employee pays the company a salary every month.
He employee at the bank.

words.meaning: A short document that lists your jobs and skills.
examples: Send your {resume} with the application form.
wrong: My resume is a list of my favorite foods.
He resumes in the box.

words.meaning: A formal meeting where someone asks you questions about a job.
examples: I have a job {interview} on Tuesday.
wrong: The interview asked me twenty questions.
She interview with the manager.

words.meaning: To give someone a higher job.
examples: They will {promote} her to manager next month.
wrong: They promoted him, so he lost his job.
He promoted to the manager.

words.meaning: One part of a large company or organization.
examples: She works in the sales {department}.
wrong: The department is a big company with no parts.
He departments in the building.

words.meaning: A person or company that pays for your services.
examples: Our {client} wants a new logo.
wrong: Our client works for us and gets a salary.
She clients the company.

words.meaning: A time when something happens later than planned.
examples: There is a one-hour {delay} at the airport.
wrong: The delay made the train arrive early.
He delay the flight.

words.meaning: To help someone remember something.
examples: Please {remind} me to call the bank.
wrong: I remind a letter to the bank.
She reminds me about to call.

words.meaning: To fix one thing to another, such as a file to an email.
examples: Please {attach} the document to your email.
wrong: I attach the document by deleting it from the email.
He attached with the file.

words.meaning: To give a document or work to someone for a decision.
examples: You must {submit} the form by noon.
wrong: I submit the form by throwing it away.
She submitted for the report.

words.meaning: To look at something again to check it.
examples: I will {review} your report tonight.
wrong: I review the report before I write it.
He reviews to the document.

words.meaning: To ask formally for a job or a place.
examples: She decided to {apply} for the new position.
wrong: I apply a new job, so they ask me to leave.
He applied to a job.

words.meaning: To give someone a job.
examples: The company will {hire} three new workers.
wrong: The company hired him, so he lost his job.
They hires many workers.

words.meaning: A set period of time when a person works.
examples: He works the night {shift} at the hospital.
wrong: My shift is a week of vacations.
She shift every night.

words.meaning: Comments that tell you how well you did something.
examples: I asked my boss for {feedback} on my presentation.
wrong: I gave my boss feedback by saying nothing at all.
He feedbacks us.

words.meaning: A lower price than the usual one.
examples: The shop gave me a ten percent {discount}.
wrong: A discount makes the price go up.
He discount a lot on shoes.

words.meaning: A paper that shows you paid for something.
examples: Keep the {receipt} in case you need to return it.
wrong: The shop gave me a receipt before I paid.
He receipts of the shop.

words.meaning: A move to a more important job.
examples: She got a {promotion} after two years.
wrong: A promotion is a move to a less important job.

words.meaning: A certificate or exam result that shows you can do something.
examples: You need a {qualification} in nursing for this job.
wrong: A qualification is a kind of vacation from work.

words.meaning: Knowledge or skill that you get from doing something for a time.
examples: He has five years of {experience} in sales.
wrong: Experience is something you can buy in a shop for ten dollars in one minute.

words.meaning: The series of jobs that a person has in their working life.
examples: She has had a long {career} in teaching.
wrong: A career is a short break between two meals.

words.meaning: The ability to do something well.
examples: Typing is a useful {skill}.
wrong: A skill is something that you cannot learn.

words.meaning: Teaching that prepares you to do a job.
examples: All new staff get a week of {training}.
wrong: Training is the act of doing nothing at work.

words.meaning: A duty to deal with something or to take care of someone.
examples: Keeping the keys is my {responsibility}.
wrong: Responsibility means you never need to do anything.

words.meaning: To say officially that you are leaving your job.
examples: He decided to {resign} and start a business.
wrong: I resign when my boss gives me a new job.

words.meaning: To stop working because you are old.
examples: My grandfather will {retire} next year.
wrong: People retire when they start their first job.

words.meaning: Without a job.
examples: He has been {unemployed} for six months.
wrong: She is unemployed, so she works full time in an office.

words.meaning: To find new people to work for a company.
examples: The shop wants to {recruit} two new assistants.
wrong: Companies recruit people when they want fewer workers.

words.meaning: A person who applies for a job or is in an election.
examples: The company interviewed five {candidates}.
wrong: A candidate is a person who has already got the job and works there.

words.meaning: A letter or statement from someone who says what you are like.
examples: My teacher wrote me a good {reference}.
wrong: A reference is a kind of tool for cutting paper.

words.meaning: A short period of work to gain experience.
examples: She did a summer {internship} at a newspaper.
wrong: An internship is a long career with a high salary.

words.meaning: The place where people do their job.
examples: Safety is important in the {workplace}.
wrong: A workplace is a place where people only sleep.

words.meaning: A time when workers refuse to work to ask for something.
examples: The drivers went on {strike} for better pay.
wrong: A strike is a day when everyone works more hours than usual by choice.

words.meaning: Money that a person earns, usually paid weekly.
examples: The workers asked for a higher {wage}.
wrong: A wage is money that you pay to a shop for bread.

words.meaning: The money that a person or family earns.
examples: Her monthly {income} is $2,000.
wrong: Income is the money you pay when you buy a bus ticket.
